✅ Acute Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Infection  

**Key Supporting Evidence:**  
- Acute onset of fatigue and jaundice (2-day duration)  
- Markedly elevated ALT (2,000 IU/L) — indicative of severe hepatocellular injury  
- Positive HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc — diagnostic of acute HBV infection  
- Negative anti-HAV IgM — excludes acute hepatitis A  
- No alternative etiologies identified (no alcohol, drugs, toxins, travel, or chronic liver disease history)

- Check remaining LFTs: AST, total/direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT, albumin, INR (to assess severity and synthetic function)

- Counsel on transmission precautions (contact, droplet, blood/body fluid precautions); screen household/sexual contacts for HBV immunity and vaccinate if non-immune

- This is a new, acute viral infection — not chronic  
- Avoid alcohol, NSAIDs, and herbal supplements until cleared

- Acute onset of fatigue and jaundice over 2 days  
- Markedly elevated ALT (2,000 IU/L), indicating severe acute hepatocellular injury  
- Positive HBsAg — required for HBV infection  
- Positive IgM anti-HBc — serologic hallmark of acute (or recent) HBV infection  
- Negative anti-HAV IgM — excludes acute hepatitis A as an alternative cause  
- No history of alcohol use, hepatotoxic drugs, toxins, travel, or chronic liver disease — reduces likelihood of competing etiologies

- Quantitative HBV DNA level (viral load) — would confirm active viral replication and help assess prognosis  
- AST level and ALT/AST ratio — supportive but not required; ALT alone is sufficient here  
- Total and direct bilirubin — to quantify degree of jaundice and cholestasis

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute Hepatitis B Virus Infection
